resolutions.rationale: The opportunity-to-character sequence is logically intelligible, while the source itself leaves the separate victim-justification condition unresolved.
The mechanism is described clearly, but the necessity and severity of serious natural suffering rest mainly on asserted counterfactual claims.
The reply directly addresses natural evil through sufferers’ and observers’ choices, yet it does not fully answer Ehrman’s victim-benefit challenge.
The move materially advances the pro explanation of natural evil, but proportionality and benefit to victims remain open parts of the burden.
The progression from suffering through repeated response choices to character formation is clear, while the claimed need for severe cases remains imprecisely bounded.
Calling serious natural evils necessary for holiness is more confident than the argument supplied, especially given the preserved victim-benefit objection.
The pastoral-versus-analytic distinction is careful, but claiming the tsunami provided opportunity for everybody involved exceeds the support presented.
The permission distinction and historical-choice argument are identifiable, but the supposed preference of nonconsenting victims is asserted without support.
The parable asks which life is best rather than merely desired, yet “surely” overstates agreement and extends chosen valuable pain toward involuntary suffering.
No separate pro adjustment is warranted because the listed explanatory bridges, strengths, and gaps are already represented in the move-level dimensions.
No separate con adjustment is warranted because the victim, natural-evil, scripture, intervention, and response challenges are already scored move by move.
